RECOMMENDATION

The Planning Commission has the following options:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. PC-2024-010, recommending City Council adoption and
  finding that the proposed Five-Year Capital Improvement Project (CIP) plan for
  fiscal years (FY) 2024-2025 through 2028-2029 is consistent with the goals,
  objectives, and policies of the General Plan and Government Code section 65103,
  and find that the project is exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act
  (CEQA).

  2. Continue the proposed five-year CIP plan and direct staff to return with additional
  information.

  3. Deny the proposed five-year CIP plan.

Option 1 is recommended.

BACKGROUND

Section 65103 of the Government Code requires that each City annually review their five-
year CIP plan for consistency with the General Plan. The purpose of the consistency
review is to ensure that capital improvement projects are not placed in locations that are
designated for other purposes under the General Plan and to ensure that the budgeted
improvements are consistent with the goals, objectives, and policies of the General Plan.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The City’s proposed Five-Year CIP plan is an effective tool used to determine the
expenditure of resources for public infrastructure. It is a short-range, five-year plan, which
identifies capital projects and related special studies, provides a planning schedule, and
identifies options for financing the program. The planning document identifies the
recommended allocation of the City’s limited resources for capital projects for FY 2024-
2025 through 2028-2029.

The proposed Five-Year CIP plan is comprised of 85 proposed projects with an
estimated total cost of $633,077. A copy of the project summary and descriptions are
attached to this report as a reference.

Staff reviewed each project listed and determined it to be consistent with the General
Plan Land Use Map and the goals, policies, and objectives of the General Plan as
discussed within Resolution No. PC-2024-010. All proposed drainage improvement
projects conform to the Master Drainage Plan and the Public Services Element of the
General Plan. The proposed circulation system improvements conform to the adopted
Circulation Element and Land Use Map of the General Plan. All proposed parks meet the
locational criteria contained in the Parks, Recreation, and Trails Element.

Once the Planning Commission has determined that the report is consistent with the
General Plan, it will be forwarded to the City Council for consideration and approval. This
is consistent with the General Plan Policy PFS1-6.10 requiring an annual update of the
CIP to prioritize funding for public works projects in accordance with the General Plan.

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

Review of the proposed Five-Year CIP plan is not an approval of the individual actions
within the Plan; it is only a determination that the Plan is in conformance with the City’s
General Plan. The individual actions described in the proposed Five-Year CIP plan are
speculative and the determination of conformance does not commit funding to any
specific project. Therefore, the proposed action is not a “Project” as defined in Section
15378(b)(4) of the CEQA Guidelines, which states that: Project does not include: The
creation of government funding mechanisms or other government fiscal activities, which
do not involve any commitment to any specific project, which may result in a potentially
significant impact on the environment.

Therefore, it has been determined that the finding of conformance with the City’s General
Plan is exempt from the requirements of the CEQA pursuant to the general rule [Section
15061(b)(3)] of the State CEQA Guidelines which states that CEQA applies only to
projects which have the potential for causing a significant physical effect on the
environment. Where it can be seen with certainty that there is no possibility that the
activity in question may have a significant physical effect on the environment, the activity
is not subject to CEQA.

   PROJECT PLANNING & DEVELOPMENT PROCESSES

Five-Year Capital Improvement Program Annual Update

The Five-Year CIP Plan is presented to the Planning Commission for their
determination as to whether it is consistent with the general plan goals and policies of
the City annually. Once the document has been reviewed and approved by the
Planning Commission, City Council is presented with a detailed report for approval in
June of each year.

Annual Capital Improvement Budget Process

The City’s annual budget process was started with a Kickoff on March 25, 2024 and
Finance had a series of meetings with department heads and staff to develop the
overall City budget. This process identified all priority operational needs, as well as
capital improvement needs. Once the budget is completed, it is recommended for
adoption by the City Council prior to the beginning of the fiscal year, which begins in
July. City management and the City Council are updated monthly on the status of CIP
projects through status reporting and meetings.

Project Phases

Individual projects may take anywhere from a few weeks to a few years to complete
depending on the complexity of the project and the source of project financing. Simple
and small projects funded with discretionary City funds may sometimes be completed in
as little as a few weeks or months. The largest and most complex projects involving a
matrix of restricted funding sources with matching requirements from other outside
sources may take several years to complete. Individual CIP projects may require any or
all the following project phases. Each phase of a complex project is regulated by
several layers of governmental agencies that may have jurisdiction over various aspects
of a project. These agencies often have many legal restrictions and requirements to
follow to complete a particular phase of a project. The major phases of a City project
are generally summarized as follows:

  1. Preliminary Concept: This phase typically includes the involvement of several
  City staff and may include the involvement of a design engineer, building
  architect, or landscape architect. The City Council is typically briefed on
  concepts involving significant projects prior to moving forward into the design
  phase.

  Page | 1
 2. Consultant Services: The expertise of specialized consultants are utilized
  regularly for professional services involving:  special studies; right-of-way
  acquisition; civil engineering design, building architectural design; geotechnical
  engineering studies; traffic engineering design and studies; landscape
  architectural design; environmental review and assessment; and special district
  formation. City Council approval is required for services over and above the City
  Manager’s designated authority and any ongoing agreement limitations.

3. Entitlements & Approvals: Most projects involve some type of entitlement or
  approval including: Planning Commission or Planning Official Site Plan Approval
  and conformance with the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) or
  federal equivalent, the National Environmental Protection Act (NEPA).

4. Design Review & Approvals: Design review and approvals may involve internal
  (Engineering and Building & Safety) approvals and/or external (outside agency)
  review and approvals (i.e. Palmdale Water District, City of Lancaster, Los
  Angeles County, Caltrans, federal agencies, etc.)

5. Utility Coordination: Many projects will involve coordination with outside utility
  agencies such as: Palmdale Water District, L.A. County Waterworks Districts,
  SBC Telephone, Southern California Gas, Southern California Edison, Adelphia,
  Los Angeles County Department of Public Works Sewer Maintenance Division,
  and the County Sanitation Districts of Los Angeles County.

6. Acquisition: Acquisitions may be made by “friendly” acquisition in which there is
  a willing buyer (City) and seller or by Eminent Domain, which involves a legal
  process and requires City Council approval.

7. Construction Contract Bid & Award: In 2010 the City of Palmdale adopted
  ordinance 1398 containing specific provisions to allow added flexibility in
  contracting for public projects. This Ordinance allows the City to consider criteria
  other than price (such as qualifications, schedule, experience, and local
  preference) when awarding a contract. Other criteria in the Ordinance have not
  changed: 1) Public works construction projects with a value of less than $30,000
  may be selected by solicitation of binding quotes from three contractors. No
  formal selection process is required. 2) Public works construction projects with a
  value of $30,000 to $149,000 are selected by an informal bid process, which
  includes, but limited to, a 10-day bid period, unsealed bids, and no published
  notice inviting bids. 3) Public works construction projects with a value of more
  than $150,000 are selected by public bid and is publicly advertised and state
  prevailing wages must be paid. In many cases, meeting state and federal legal
  requirements, may add an additional 10% to 25% to the project cost and require
  the formal bidding process.

  Page | 2
 8. Construction Contract Administration: After a contract is executed between the
  city and a contractor, the assigned project manager and public works inspector
  will provide construction contract administration duties. The duration of project
  construction may be as little as a few days to more than a year for larger
  projects. The contract administration team ensures that the contractor adheres
  to all regulations and contract provisions required by federal, state and local law.
  Typically, for larger construction projects the city will use a consultant to provide
  construction management of the contractor and to assist project managers in
  keeping the project on schedule.

9. Legal: Legal services are required on most projects and may include: review of
  service agreements, construction cash contracts, bidding process, sub-contractor
  stop notices, individual claims on projects during & after construction, contractor
  disputes, and acquisition related issues.

10. Project Close-out: Once the project construction is complete, there are often
  many financial, legal and other aspects to closing out a project file including:
  filing legal Notices of Completion, processing all final payments, preparing all
  grant or financing related project reports, and final organization and preparation
  of the file for future auditing.

Access

Access would be provided via three driveways: one from Trade Center Drive, one from
5th Street West, and one from Technology Drive. The proposed driveway on Trade Center
Drive, located in the northwest corner of the site, would be 42 feet wide and would provide
access to both passenger vehicles and trucks. The proposed driveway on 5th Street West
located in the northeast corner of the site would be 41 feet wide, providing access to both
passenger vehicles and trucks. The proposed driveway on Technology Drive located in
the southern portion of the site would be 28 feet wide and would be limited to passenger
vehicles. Onsite circulation would be provided by a 28-foot-wide internal driveway around

contemplated and analyzed for the parcel(s) in the GP EIR and complies with the
associated standards applicable to that development density (State CEQA Guidelines
Section 15183(i)(2)). Development density standards can include the number of dwelling
units per acre, the number of people in a given area, floor area ratio (FAR), and other
measures of building intensity, building height, size limitations, and use restrictions. The
CEQA Streamlining analysis determined that the proposed project meets the
requirements for a CEQA Exemption pursuant to Section 15183 of the CEQA Guidelines

1 INTRODUCTION
1.1 OVERVIEW OF CEQA GUIDELINES SECTION 15183
This CEQA Streamlining analysis evaluates whether the potential environmental impacts of the Project are
addressed in the City of Palmdale General Plan Update 2045 Final Environmental Impact Report (GP EIR)
(State Clearinghouse Number 2021060494) pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA)
Guidelines (CEQA Guidelines) Section 15183 (CEQA Streamlining Checklist).
As set forth in California Public Resources Code (PRC) Section 21083.3 and State CEQA Guidelines Section
15183, projects that are “consistent with the development density established by the existing zoning,
community plan or general plan policies for which an EIR was certified shall not require additional
environmental review, except as might be necessary to examine whether there are project-specific significant
effects which are peculiar to the project or its site” (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15183(a) and PRC
Section 21083.3(b)). The State CEQA Guidelines further state that “[i]f an impact is not peculiar to the parcel
or to the project, has been addressed as a significant effect in the prior EIR, or can be substantially mitigated
by the imposition of uniformly applied development policies or standards […] then an additional EIR need
not be prepared for the project solely on the basis of that impact” (State CEQA Guidelines Section
15183(c)).”
In Wal-Mart Stores, Inc. v. City of Turlock, 138 Cal.App.4th 273 (2006), the court stated, “The foregoing
construction of the terms “peculiar to” and “project-specific” promotes efficiency by reducing delay and
needless paperwork and, therefore, is consistent with the purpose underlying the streamlined review of
Guidelines section 15183.”
The court went on to state that “Applying these definitions, a physical change in the environment will be
peculiar to the [Project] if that physical change belongs exclusively or especially to the [Project] or if it is
characteristic of only the [Project].” For example, impacts related to archaeological resources are not
peculiar to the proposed project, since archaeological impacts with mitigation are common with many
development projects in the state.
Similarly in Gilroy Citizens for Responsible Planning v. City of Gilroy, 140 Cal.App.4th 911 (2006) the court
found that because the project would have significant air quality impacts and because the General Plan EIR
concluded the same, there was nothing peculiar about the project. There is nothing peculiar about a project
with significant impacts if the EIR already analyzed and determined those projects to be significant.
Most recently, in Lucas v. City of Pomona (2023) the Court of Appeal held that “[b]ecause Guidelines section
15183 requires an agency to examine whether a project’s environmental effects were analyzed as
significant impacts in a prior EIR on a general plan or zoning action with which the project is consistent…. the
substantial evidence standard applies.”

1.2 PALMDALE GENERAL PLAN 2045 ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT REPORT
In 2022, the City of Palmdale adopted The City of Palmdale General Plan Update 2045 (GP) and certified
the GP Final EIR. The GP consists of the following twelve elements that together meet State requirements for
a general plan: Land Use and Community Design; Circulation and Mobility; Economic Development; Military
Compatibility; Equitable and Healthy Communities; Parks, Recreation, and Open Space; Conservation; Public
Facilities, Services, and Infrastructure; Safety; Sustainability, Climate Action, and Resilience; Air Quality; and
Noise.
The GP EIR evaluated the potential environmental effects from implementation of the General Plan Update
(GP), and development pursuant to the GP is subject to mitigation measures identified in the GP EIR and the

1.3 PROJECT OVERVIEW
The Project proposes to develop the 12.74-acre site with a 281,935-square-foot (SF) warehouse building
with office space and truck trailer parking. The Project site is currently undeveloped and supports vegetation
consisting of shrubs and grasses. The proposed warehouse building would be one story with a maximum
height of 45 feet, and result in a FAR of 0.5. Additional improvements would include landscaping, sidewalks,
utility connections, implementation of stormwater facilities, and pavement of parking areas and drive lanes.
Approvals required for the Project include a Conditional Use Permit (CUP), Site Plan Review (SPR), and a Lot
Merger.

1.4 APPLICABILITY OF STATE CEQA GUIDELINES SECTION 15183
As set forth in State CEQA Guidelines Section 15183(d), the additional environmental review streamlining
applies to projects which meet the following conditions:
  1. The project is consistent with:
  (A) A community plan adopted as part of a general plan,
  (B) A zoning action which zoned or designated the parcel on which the project would be located
  to accommodate a particular density of development, or
  (C) A general plan of a local agency, and
  2. An EIR was certified by the lead agency for the zoning action, the community plan, or the general
  plan.
Additionally, the environmental review streamlining applies only to the extent that all feasible mitigation
measures identified in the applicable general plan are implemented by the public agency with jurisdiction
to require such mitigation measures (State CEQA Guidelines Section 15183(e)).
The GP EIR analyzed the impacts of buildout of the GP land use plan. As discussed in this Streamlining
Checklist, the Project is consistent with the land uses identified for the site in the GP. The Project site has a
GP land use designation of Regional Commercial (RC). The RC land use designation is intended to
accommodate retail and service uses attracting consumers from a regional market area, and film uses within
the LA County secondary zone. The RC land use designation allows for warehouse uses with the approval of
a CUP. The Project would develop the 12.74-acre site with one industrial warehouse building with a total
building area of 281,935 SF, resulting in a FAR of 0.5, which is consistent with the 1.0 max FAR identified in
the GP EIR. As such, the GP EIR adequately anticipated and analyzed the impacts of development consistent
with the GP, identified applicable mitigation measures necessary to reduce impacts of such development,
and required implementation of the mitigation measures where applicable. The Project follows and
implements that guidance without triggering any new or unanticipated significant impacts. The Project,
therefore, qualifies for an exemption from additional environmental review as set forth in State CEQA
Guidelines Section 15183.

3.1 PROJECT OVERVIEW
The Project proposes the development of a 281,935 SF warehouse building on a 12.74-acre site with office
space and truck trailer parking. Additional improvements would include landscaping, sidewalks, utility
connections, implementation of stormwater facilities, pavement of parking areas and drive aisles, and

3.2 PROJECT FEATURES
Building Summary
The proposed warehouse building would be one story and approximately 45 feet tall with a total building
area of 281,935 SF. The Project site is 12.74 acres, which results in a FAR of 0.5. The warehouse would
have a building footprint of 274,935 SF of warehouse space, 3,000 SF of ground floor office space, and
4,000 SF of mezzanine office space.
The Project would have frontages along Trade Center Drive to the west, Technology Drive to the south and
5th Street West to the east. The building would be set back approximately 10 feet from the northern property
line, approximately 10 feet from the eastern property line, approximately 10 feet from the western
property line, and approximately 20 feet from the southern property line.
As shown in Figure 3-2, Elevations, the proposed Project would establish a quality architectural presence
along Technology Drive and Trade Center Drive through emphasis on building finish materials and consistent
material usage and color scheme of blues and grays. Trees would be incorporated within the perimeter
landscaping in order to screen the building and loading docks.
Parking Lot and Loading Dock Summary
The warehouse would include 35 dock doors located along the northern side of the building and 54 trailer
parking spaces north of the building adjacent to the northern property line. Additionally, 172 passenger
vehicle spaces, including 35 electric vehicle (EV) and six accessible (ADA) spaces, would be provided for
employees along the west, east, and south sides of the building as well as in the northwest and northeast
portions of the site. The Project would also provide bike parking for 18 bikes.
Landscaping and Fencing
The proposed Project includes 104,269 SF of ornamental landscaping that would cover approximately 19
percent of the site, exceeding the 10 percent landscaping requirement for the overall site, as shown in Figure
3-3, Landscape Plan. Proposed landscaping includes 36-inch and 24-inch box trees, 15-gallon trees, various
5-gallon shrubs and accent plants, and 1-gallon groundcover plants. The larger trees would be placed
around the perimeter along frontage roads to screen the proposed building, detention basin, and parking
and loading areas from off-site viewpoints on Technology Drive, Trade Center Drive, and 5th Street West.
Project landscaping would be consistent with the City of Palmdale Municipal Code Section 17.86.010,
Landscaping Requirements.
An 8-foot wrought iron fence is proposed on the northern Project boundary adjacent to the trailer parking
stalls. In addition, a 0 to 10-foot (height varies) retaining wall would be constructed along the northern end
of the Project site; and a 2 to 4-foot (height varies) retaining wall would be constructed along the eastern
property line adjacent to 5th Street West and in the southeast corner of the Project site.

Access and Circulation
Access would be provided via three driveways: one from Trade Center Drive, one from 5th Street West,
and one from Technology Drive. The proposed driveway on Trade Center Drive, located in the northwest
corner of the site, would be 42 feet wide and would provide access to both passenger vehicles and trucks.
The proposed driveway on 5th Street West located in the northeast corner of the site would be 41 feet wide,
providing access to both passenger vehicles and trucks. The proposed driveway on Technology Drive located
in the southern portion of the site would be 28 feet wide and would be limited to passenger vehicles. Onsite
circulation would be provided by a 28-foot-wide internal driveway around the building that would double
as fire access. Truck traffic generated by the Project would primarily use SR-14 to Technology Drive to enter
the Project site.
Access to trailer stalls and loading dock areas would be controlled through the use of gates. The development
would include one metal manually operated gate at each entrance/exit of the truck loading area, for a
total of two gates. Each gate includes knox padlocks for fire department access.
Infrastructure Improvements
Water and Sewer Improvement
The Project would install new onsite water lines that connect to the existing 12-inch water line along Trade
Center Drive, the existing 16-inch water line along Technology Drive, and the existing 12-inch water line
along 5th Street West. In addition, the Project would install new onsite sewer lines that connect to the existing
8-inch sewer line along Trade Center Drive, the existing 12-inch sewer line along Technology Drive, and the
existing 8-inch sewer line along 5th Street West.
Drainage Improvements
The Project would install new onsite storm drain connections. Stormwater would be collected using a system
of catch basins and roof drains that route flows to underground pipes. All stormwater runoff would be
conveyed to a proposed 4,783-SF detention basin at the northeast corner of the Project site. Overflow would
drain into existing City stormwater drains.
Street Improvements
The Project would include the construction of a raised median along Technology Drive, south of the 28-foot
driveway.

3.3 CONSTRUCTION AND PHASING
Construction activities would occur over one phase and include site preparation, grading, building
construction, paving, and architectural coatings. Grading of soils is expected to result in no import or export;
therefore, the site earthwork would be balanced. Construction is expected to begin June 2024 and would
occur over 12 months within the hours allowable by the City of Palmdale Municipal Code Section 8.28.030,
which states that construction shall occur only between the hours of 6:30 AM and 8:00 PM, except on Sundays.

3.4 OPERATIONAL CHARACTERISTICS
The Project would operate as a speculative high cube warehouse. Typical operational characteristics include
employees traveling to and from the site, delivery of materials and supplies to the site, and truck loading
and unloading. Operation is assumed to be 24 hours a day, seven days a week. No cold storage is assumed
for this Project. Operation of the proposed Project would require approximately 331 employees.

a) Have a substantial adverse effect on a scenic vista?
No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on pages 4.1-6 through 4.1-7 and was determined
to have a less than significant impact. Scenic vistas provide expansive views of highly valued landscape for
the benefit of the public. The GP EIR notes that scenic vistas of the desert and local mountains are the
predominant scenic vistas in Palmdale. Distant views of the San Gabriel Mountains, Sierra Pelona Mountains,
and Tehachapi Mountains are available across the Planning Area, but the best views of these mountains are
from large areas of unobstructed open space. In other areas throughout the City, views of the mountains are
fully to partially obstructed by existing trees and buildings.
The Project site is currently undeveloped with vegetation consisting of shrubs and grasses. A hotel and
associated parking lot exist on the northeast corner of the lot. The Proposed Project consists of the
development of a new one-story warehouse with office space and truck trailer parking on a 12.74-acre site.
The total building area would be 281,935 SF and would result in a FAR of 0.5.
There are no adopted scenic vistas in the Planning Area. Views of the Gabriel Mountains and the Sierra
Pelona Mountains are available from the Project site to the southeast and to the west, respectively. However,
the views are largely obstructed by existing buildings. Therefore, future views after development of the
Project would be similar to existing views.
The GP EIR determined that future development projects under the GP would not have a substantial negative
impact on public views or scenic vistas. Further, the policies included in the GP set building height limits in
specific areas and for industrial land uses. Development of the proposed warehouse would require review
under the City’s standard development review procedures to ensure that the development is consistent with
the policies listed in the GP as well as design standards contained in the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC).
Therefore, the proposed development would not have substantial impacts on public views or scenic vistas. As
such, the Project would result in less than significant impacts on views of scenic resources (distant mountain
views), and the Project is consistent with surrounding uses and City development standards. As such, the
proposed Project is consistent with the findings contained in the GP EIR, and the Project would result in no
new impact.

criteria to determine whether a Project would be consistent or in conflict with any applicable maintenance

A Project is non-conforming if it conflicts with or delays implementation of any applicable attainment or
maintenance plan. A Project is conforming if it complies with all applicable District rules and regulations,
complies with all proposed control measures that are not yet adopted from the applicable plan(s), and is
consistent with the growth forecasts in the applicable plan(s) (or is directly included in the applicable plan).
Conformity with growth forecasts can be established by demonstrating that the Project is consistent with the
land use plan that was used to generate the growth forecast. An example of a non-conforming Project would
be one that increases the gross number of dwelling units, increases the number of trips, and/or increases the
overall vehicle miles traveled in an affected area (relative to the applicable land use plan).
AVAQMD has adopted two attainment plans, the Federal Particulate Matter Attainment Plan and Ozone
Attainment Plan. These plans have been set to move the MDAB from federal and state nonattainment status
for PM10 and Ozone to federal and state attainment status. These plans were created based on the future
growth assumptions based on existing general plan land uses (GPLUs), which assumptions for those land uses
were provided by local governments.
Additionally, the Project site is within the Southern California Council of Governments (SCAG) area. The
SCAG 2045 Regional Transportation Plan/Sustainable Communities Strategy (RTP/SCS) analyzes the
impacts of the assumed buildout of the SCAG region. This is done by using the GPLU information provided
by the multiple jurisdictions within the SCAG region.
Therefore, if the proposed Project is consistent with the existing GPLU, the proposed Project would be
consistent with SCAG’s RTP/SCS growth assumptions. The proposed Project is consistent with the allowable
land uses in the existing GPLU of Regional Commercial (RC). Therefore, the Project would not conflict with
the analyzed growth assumptions in the AVAQMD attainment plans and SCAG RTP/SCS and have a less
than significant impact. As such, the proposed Project is consistent with the findings contained in the GP EIR

The MDAB is designated as nonattainment for O3 and PM2.5 for federal standards and nonattainment for
O3, PM10, and PM2.5 for State standards. The AVAQMD’s nonattainment status is attributed to the region’s
development history. Past, present, and future development projects contribute to the region’s adverse air
quality impacts on a cumulative basis. By its very nature, air pollution is largely a cumulative impact. No
single project is sufficient in size to, by itself, result in nonattainment of ambient air quality standards. Instead,
a project’s individual emissions contribute to existing cumulatively significant adverse air quality impacts. If
a project’s contribution to the cumulative impact is considerable, then the project’s impact on air quality would
be considered significant. In developing thresholds of significance for air pollutants, the AVAQMD considered
the emission levels for which a project’s individual emissions would be cumulatively considerable. If a project
exceeds the identified significance thresholds, its emissions would be cumulatively considerable, resulting in
significant adverse air quality impacts to the region’s existing air quality conditions.

c) Expose sensitive receptors to substantial pollutant concentrations?
No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on page 4.3-20 and was determined to have a less
than significant impact.
The AVAQMD has established an incidence rate of ten (10) persons per million as the maximum acceptable
incremental cancer risk and/or a Hazard index (Hi) (non-cancer) greater than 1.0 due to exposures to
sensitive receptors from substantial pollutant concentration. Exposures below the 10 in one million cancer risk
thresholds are not likely to be associated with any adverse health effects and are considered to be less than
significant. Non-carcinogenic risk is expressed as a hazard index, which is calculated by comparing the
exposure to the reference level via a ratio (i.e., the exposure divided by the appropriate chronic or acute
value). Exposures below the reference level (a hazard index of 1.0) are not likely to be associated with any
adverse health effects and are considered to be less than significant.
The AVAQMD relies on the guidance from the South Coast Air Quality Management District (SCAQMD) to
determine cumulative impacts. The SCAQMD has recognized that there is typically insufficient information to
quantitatively evaluate the cumulative contributions of multiple projects because each project applicant has
no control over nearby projects. The SCAQMD has published a report on addressing cumulative impacts
from air pollution: White Paper on Potential Control Strategies to Address Cumulative Impacts from Air
Pollution 1. The SCAQMD considers projects exceeding the project-specific significance thresholds as a
cumulatively considerable impact. Therefore, the project-specific (cancer risk and non-cancer hazards) and
cumulative significance thresholds are the same. As a result, projects that do not exceed the project-specific
thresholds are not considered to be cumulatively significant.

placed over the Project site area to complete the receptor network. The nearest sensitive receptor was

in the GP EIR, 32 special-status animal species and 43 special-status plant species have been observed or
have the potential to occur in the Planning Area. Furthermore, existing ornamental trees and vegetation have
the potential to support nesting birds that are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) and/or
the California Fish and Game Code (CFGC). While development that could alter biological habitat could
occur in portions of the Planning Area, all development would be subject to the provisions of the various
federal and State natural resources regulations. Furthermore, implementation of the goals and policies listed
in the GP would ensure that projects would be completed in accordance with protecting and preserving
sensitive ecological areas and protecting special status species. The GP EIR noted that individual
development projects would be subject to provisions of applicable federal and State natural resources
regulations, which would require biological studies for projects where potential habitat exists.
Electronic inventory searches conducted as part of the BRA prepared for this Project (ELMT Consulting, 2023)
identified eight special status plant species, twenty-five special-status wildlife species, and no special-status
plant communities that have the potential to occur within the Project site. The BRA also included a field
investigation conducted on July 13, 2023. No special-status plants or animal species were encountered
during the field investigation. The BRA concluded that the Project site has low potential to support special-
status plants or animal species based on habitat requirements, availability and quality of habitat, and
proximity of the site to known occurrences.
Nonetheless, due to regional significance, the potential occurrence of burrowing owl, desert tortoise, and
Mojave ground squirrel are discussed in further detail below.
Burrowing Owl
The burrowing owl is currently listed as a California Species of Special Concern and federally protected by
the MBTA. No burrowing owls or recent signs (i.e., pellets, feathers, castings, or whitewash) were observed
during the field investigation. The Project is characterized by low-growing plant species that allows for line-
of-sight observation, which is favored by burrowing owls. In addition, two suitable burrows measuring less
than four inches were observed during the field surveys, but the burrows did not present signs of use by
burrowing owls. However, the site is surrounded by electrical poles, tall buildings, and streetlights that
provide perching opportunities for large raptors that prey on burrowing owls, which would reduce the

likelihood that burrowing owl would establish on-site. Therefore, the Project site was determined to have low
potential to support burrowing owls.
As part of the nesting bird surveys done in accordance with GP Mitigation Measure BIO-1, burrowing owl
pre-construction clearance surveys would be conducted prior to any ground disturbance or vegetation
removal to ensure that burrowing owls remain absent from the Project site. Furthermore, the proposed Project
would implement the GP goals and policies that encourage the conservation and protection of natural
resources and reduce potential impacts to special-status species and sensitive habitats. Overall, with
implementation of Mitigation Measure BIO-1, the proposed Project would have less than significant impact
to burrowing owl. As such, the proposed Project would result in no new impact and is consistent with the GP
EIR.
Desert Tortoise
No live desert tortoises, suitable burrows, or other signs were observed during the field investigation. The
desert tortoise typically prefers the Mojavean desert scrub habitat. The habitat at the Project site rubber
rabbitbrush scrub plant community supported, which is not the typical forage community preferred by desert
tortoise. Additionally, the Project site is separated from suitable habitat by existing development, including
roadways which support regular traffic. As such, desert tortoise is presumed to be absent from the Project
site.
Mojave Ground Squirrel
The Project site is within the historic range of Mohave ground squirrel (MGS); however, the site is not located
within any core areas, nor is it located within or immediately adjacent to any corridors or other known
populations. Even though the Project site supports plant communities suitable for MGS, the species has not
been detected in the immediate vicinity of the Project site during protocol surveys. The closest documented
MGS was captured approximately 18 miles northeast of the Project site.
Overall, the MGS prefers habitat characterized by a diverse shrub component that contains hoary saltbush,
spiny hopsage, and winterfat. The Project site is characterized by low diversity in shrub components and
does not include the plant species that are considered important forage for MGS. Further, no wildlife
corridors are expected to exist between the closest core MGS population and the project site because the
maximum document movement of MGS is 3.9 miles.
The Project site is surrounded by development including heavily trafficked roadways and commercial
structures. Further, the site has been subject to routine disturbance from adjacent development, illegal
dumping, and off-highway recreational vehicle use. Therefore, while the site provides native habitat, the
disturbances associated with agricultural activities and the airport, and location from core populations
reduces the potential for MGS to occupy the project site. Therefore, based on habitat requirements for
Mohave ground squirrel, known distributions, site conditions, and regional trapping studies, the MGS is
presumed absent from the project site.
Nesting Birds
As discussed above, nesting birds are protected pursuant to the MBTA and CFGC (Sections 3503, 3503.5,
3511, and 3513 prohibit the take, possession, or destruction of birds, their nests, or eggs). Nesting birds
could be impacted by development projects that involve the trimming or removal of vegetation and trees or
where construction occurs near trees and vegetation. The Project site and surrounding area provide suitable
nesting opportunities for year-round and seasonal avian residents, as well as migrating songbirds. No active
nests were observed on-site during the field investigation; however, several birds exhibiting nesting behavior
were observed in adjacent areas. No raptors are expected to nest on-site due to lack of suitable nesting

No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on page 4.7-16 and was determined to have a less
than significant impact with compliance of applicable building codes. As discussed on page 4.7-16 of the
GP EIR, all future development projects would be subject to the City’s codes and requirements relative to
geotechnical impacts. Additionally, all new development would be constructed in compliance with Chapter
8.04 of the PMC, which requires an engineering geology and/or geotechnical engineering report when the

Consistent with the findings of the GP EIR, a Project-specific Geotechnical Investigation was conducted in
October 2023 (NorCal Engineering, 2023; Appendix D). As described above, the Project site is flat and
does not contain nor is adjacent to any significant slope of hillside area. The Project would not create slopes.
Thus, on or off-site landslides would not occur from implementation of the Project.
Lateral spreading is a type of liquefaction-induced ground failure associated with the lateral displacement
of surficial blocks of sediment resulting from liquefaction in a subsurface layer. Once liquefaction transforms
the subsurface layer into a fluid mass, gravity plus the earthquake inertial forces may cause the mass to
move downslope towards a free face (such as a river channel or an embankment). Lateral spreading may
cause large horizontal displacements and such movement typically damages pipelines, utilities, bridges, and
structures.
The soil types found at the Project site are described in the Geotechnical Investigation. At depths ranging
from one to eight feet below ground surface (BGS), the soil types are characterized by a brown, sandy clay
to a fine to coarse grained, silty to slightly clayey sand; these soils are soft/loose to stiff/dense and damp
to moist. The soils at the Project site do not possess characteristics conducive to lateral spreading or
liquefaction. Therefore, the Project site is not susceptible to liquefaction or lateral spreading (NorCal
Engineering, 2023). As such, with compliance of the mandatory CBC requirements, impacts related to
liquefaction and lateral spreading would be less than significant.

No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on page 4.7-17 and was determined to have a less
than significant impact with compliance of the requirements of the CBC. Expansive soils contain clay particles
that swell when wet and shrink when dry. Foundations constructed on expansive soils are subjected to forces
caused by the swelling and shrinkage of the soils and could result in heaving and cracking of buildings and
foundations. The majority of the Planning Area consists of soils that have little or no swelling potential.
However, the Planning Area does contain expansive soils. As described in the GP EIR, Development projects
constructed on expansive soils could be subject to damage or could become unstable when the underlying
soil shrinks or swells.
The Geotechnical Investigation found that the Project site contains silty sand soils with an expansion index of
3 and sandy clay soils with an expansion index of 62 (NorCal Engineering, 2023). Soils with an expansion
index greater than 20 are considered expansive according to Section 1803.5.3 of the CBD. As such, the
Project site contains expansive soils. However, the Project would comply with the CBC requirements to address
soil-related hazards. In cases where soil remediation is not feasible, the CBC requires structural reinforcement
of foundations to resist the forces of expansive soils. Compliance with the requirements of the CBC would
reduce impacts related to expansive soils to a less than significant level. In addition, the Geotechnical
Investigation contains expansive soil guidelines to assist the developer in design and maintenance of projects
on expansive soils. The guidelines include controlling irrigation around building foundations and keeping
drainage away from structures and pavement.

Expansive Soil Guidelines, the proposed Project would be safe from excessive settlements under the
anticipated design loading and conditions. Thus, with adherence to the requirements of the CBC and
recommendations in the Geotechnical Investigation, impacts related to expansive soils would be less than
significant and no new impacts would occur from the Project. As such, the proposed Project is consistent with
the findings contained in the GP EIR.

f)  Directly or indirectly destroy a unique paleontological resource or site or unique geologic feature?
No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on page 4.7-18 through 4.7-19 and was determined
to have a less than significant impact with implementation of mitigation. Consistent with the findings of the
GP EIR, a project-specific Paleontological Resource Assessment was conducted by BFSA Environmental
Services in June 2023 (Appendix E). The Paleontological Resource Assessment included a pedestrian field
survey and review of paleontological literature and fossil locality records for prior projects within or in the
vicinity of the Project site. The paleontological field survey was conducted on May 22, 2023. No
paleontological resources or evidence indicating the presence of paleontological resources were identified
during the field survey. The Project site was found to have been subject to previous grading. However,
records search indicated that significant fossils have been previously discovered within the Project site. Fossils
previously discovered within the Project site and within a one-mile radius consist of early Holocene and late
Pleistocene-aged lizards, birds, and mammals, including rodents, rabbits, and unidentifiable mammalian
remains. Furthermore, elements of a Columbian mammoth were collected from one site within the perimeter
radius, immediately west of the Project site.
The geologic units underlying the Project site are late to middle Pleistocene-aged old alluvial fan deposits
consisting of silt, sand, and gravel, surrounded by various younger alluvial deposits. Pleistocene alluvial and
alluvial fan deposits in the Inland Empire are accorded a high paleontological resource sensitivity because
they often yield important Ice Age terrestrial vertebrate fossils. The Paleontological Assessment concludes
that there is very high probability that significant fossils would be present at the Project site due to previous
significant discoveries within and near the Project site (BFSA, 2023b). Earthmoving activities like grading and
excavation would adversely impact undiscovered fossils. Therefore, full-time monitoring of alluvial fan
deposits during excavation or grading activities starting at the surface would be implemented.
The proposed Project is required to follow the goals and policies in the GP to minimize impacts to
paleontological resources. Policy CON-8.4 requires that new development preserve significant historic,
paleontological, or archaeological resources. A PRIMP which outlines monitoring and treatment methods to
identify and protect previously undiscovered paleontological resources was prepared on February 7,
2024to satisfy the requirements of Policy CON-8.4 and GP EIR Mitigation Measure GEO-1. The PRIMP
follows the City’s guidelines and the recommendations of the Society of Vertebrate Paleontology (SVP).
These include attendance by a qualified paleontologist at the preconstruction meeting to consult with the
grading and excavation contractors, monitoring to inspect for paleontological resources during the
excavation of previously undisturbed deposits, and salvage and recovery of paleontological resources.
Implementation of the PRIMP consistent with GP EIR Mitigation Measure GEO-1 would reduce Project impacts
to paleontological resources to less than significant. Therefore, the Project is consistent with the findings
contained in the GP EIR impacts and would result in no new impacts that would directly or indirectly destroy
a unique paleontological resource or site or unique geologic feature.

Summary of Impacts Identified in the GP EIR
The GP EIR discussed hazards and hazardous materials impacts on pages 4.9-1 through 4.9-27 and
determined impacts would be less than significant with compliance and/or adherence to Federal, State, and
local regulation, and goals and policies in the GP. No mitigation measures related to hazards and hazardous
materials are recommended in the GP EIR.
Project-Specific Impacts
This section is based on the Phase I Environmental Site Assessment, prepared October 2023 by HEI
Corporation (HEI Corporation, 2023), and included as Appendix F.
a) Create a significant hazard to the public or the environment through the routine transport, use, or
  disposal of hazardous materials?
No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on pages 4.9-18 through 4.9-20 and was
determined to have a less than significant impact with compliance with applicable State and Federal
regulations. A hazardous material is defined as any material that, due to its quantity, concentration, or
physical or chemical characteristics, poses a significant present or potential hazard to human health and
safety or to the environment if released into the workplace or environment. Hazardous materials include, but
are not limited to, hazardous substances, hazardous wastes, and any material that a business or the local
implementing agency has a reasonable basis for believing would be injurious to the health and safety of
persons or harmful to the environment if released into the workplace or the environment. Hazardous wastes
require special handling and disposal because of their potential to damage public health and the
environment.
Construction
Heavy construction equipment (e.g., dozers, excavators, tractors) would be operated for construction of the
proposed Project. The equipment would be fueled and maintained by petroleum‐based substances such as
diesel fuel, gasoline, oil, and hydraulic fluid, which are considered hazardous if improperly stored, handled,
or transported. Other materials used, such as paints, adhesives, and solvents, could also result in accidental
releases or spills that could pose risks to people and the environment. These risks are standard on all
construction sites, and the proposed Project would not cause greater risks than would occur on other similar
construction sites.
Additionally, construction contractors would be required to comply with federal, state, and local laws and
regulations regarding the transport, use, and storage of hazardous materials. Applicable laws and
regulations include CCR, Title 8 Section 1529 (pertaining to ACM) and Section 1532.1 (pertaining to LBP);
CFR, Title 40, Part 61, Subpart M (pertaining to ACM); CCR, Title 23, Chapter 16 (pertaining to UST); CFR,
Title 29 - Hazardous Waste Control Act; CFR, Title 49, Chapter I; and Hazardous Materials Transportation
Act requirements as imposed by the USDOT, CalOSHA, CalEPA and DTSC.
Construction activities would require a SWPPP, which is mandated by the NPDES General Construction Permit
and enforced by the Lahontan Regional Water Quality Control Board (LRWQCB). The SWPPP would include

environment during construction, including, but not limited to:

•  Establishing a dedicated area for fuel storage and refueling activities that includes secondary
  containment protection measures and spill control supplies;
•  Following manufacturers’ recommendations on the use, storage, and disposal of chemical products used
  in construction;
•  Avoiding overtopping construction equipment fuel tanks;
•  Properly containing and removing grease and oils during routine maintenance of equipment; and
•  Properly disposing of discarded containers of fuels and other chemicals.
Mandatory compliance with applicable laws and regulations related to the routine transport, use, and
disposal of hazardous materials during construction activities at the Project site would limit potentially
significant hazards to construction workers, the public, and the environment. Impacts would be less than
significant, and no new impact would occur.
Operation
The Project involves the operation of a new warehouse facility with a total building area of 281,935 SF,
including 7,000 SF of office space and 168,424 SF of warehouse space. Operations of the new development
would involve routine use of hazardous materials including solvents, lubricants, cleaning agents, paints,
pesticides, batteries, fertilizers, and aerosol cans. These types of materials are not acutely hazardous and
would only be used and stored in limited quantities. The normal routine use of these hazardous materials
products pursuant to existing regulations would not result in a significant hazard to people or the environment
in the vicinity of the Project. These materials would be used, stored, and disposed of in accordance with
applicable regulations and standards (such as CFR, Title 49, Chapter I; CCR, Title 8; CFR, Title 40, Part 263)
that are enforced by the USEPA, USDOT, CalEPA, CalOSHA, DTSC).
Under California Health and Safety Code Section 25531 et seq., CalEPA requires businesses operating with
a regulated substance that exceeds a specified threshold quantity to register with a managing local agency,
known as the Certified Unified Program Agency (CUPA). Additionally, businesses are required to provide
workers with training on the safe use, handling, and storage of hazardous materials. Businesses are also
required to maintain equipment and supplies for containing and cleaning up spills of hazardous materials
that can be safely contained and cleaned by onsite workers and to immediately notify emergency response
agencies in the event of a hazardous materials release that cannot be safely contained and cleaned up by
onsite personnel. Additionally, GP Policy SE-3.4 would require the proposed Project to transport hazardous
materials along designated routes that minimize risks to the public and sensitive environmental areas.
Compliance with existing laws, regulations, Local Hazard Mitigation Plan, and GP Safety Element Policies
governing hazards and hazardous materials would result in less than significant impacts related the routine
transport, use, and disposal of the hazardous materials.
Therefore, operation of the Project would not result in a significant hazard to the public or to the environment
through the routine transport, use, or disposal of hazardous waste, and impacts would be less than significant.
As such, the proposed Project is consistent with the findings contained in the GP EIR impacts, and the Project
would result in no new impact.

a) Violate any water quality standards or waste discharge requirements or otherwise substantially

No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on page 4.10-11 through 4.10-13 and was
determined to have a less than significant impact with compliance of applicable laws and regulations and
implementation of the GP goals and policies.
Construction
Construction of the Project would require grading and excavation of soils, which would loosen sediment, and
then have the potential to mix with surface water runoff and degrade water quality. Pollutants of concern
during Project construction include sediments, trash, petroleum products, concrete waste (dry and wet),
sanitary waste, and chemicals. During construction activities, excavated soil would be exposed, and there
would be an increased potential for soil erosion and transport of sediment downstream compared to existing
conditions. During a storm event, soil erosion could occur at an accelerated rate. In addition, construction-
related pollutants, such as chemicals, liquid, and petroleum products (e.g., paints, solvents, and fuels), and
concrete-related waste, could be spilled, leaked, or transported via stormwater runoff into adjacent
drainages and into downstream receiving waters.
Construction of the Project would disturb more than one acre of soil; therefore, the proposed Project would
be required to obtain coverage under the NPDES General Permit for Discharges of Storm Water Associated
with Construction Activity. Construction activity subject to this permit includes clearing, grading, and ground
disturbances such as trenching, stockpiling, or excavation. The Construction General Permit requires
implementation of a SWPPP that is required to identify all potential sources of pollution that are reasonably
expected to affect the quality of storm water discharges from the construction site. The SWPPP would
generally contain a site map showing the construction perimeter, proposed buildings, stormwater collection
and discharge points, general pre- and post-construction topography, drainage patterns across the site, and
adjacent roadways. The SWPPP would also include construction BMPs. The SWPPP would include a
combination of erosion control measures to reduce, prevent, or minimize soil erosion from Project-related
grading and construction activities, such as fiber rolls, fencing, and watering. In addition, the Project applicant
would be required to complete a soil management report in order to reduce run off, per the conditions in
Chapter 14.05 Section 14.05.080 of the PMC.
Through compliance with mandatory Clean Water Act and PMC requirements and applicable GP goals and
policies, potential water quality degradation associated with construction activities would be minimized, and
impacts would be less than significant.
Operation
The proposed Project includes the operation of a high cube warehouse, which would introduce the potential
for pollutants such as chemicals from cleaners, pesticides and sediment from landscaping, trash and debris,
and oil and grease from vehicles and trucks. These pollutants could potentially discharge into surface waters
and result in degradation of water quality. However, through compliance with GP goal CON-6 and other

body of water is Lake Palmdale, approximately 2.75 miles to the southeast. According to the GP EIR, the

Construction vibration analysis discusses the level of human annoyance using vibration levels in RMS (VdB)
and assesses the potential for building damage using vibration levels in PPV (in/sec). This is because vibration
levels calculated in RMS velocity are best for characterizing human response to building vibration, while
calculating vibration levels in PPV is best for characterizing the potential for damage.
Table N-4 shows the maximum PPV and VdB values at 25 feet from the construction vibration source. As
shown in Table N-4, large bulldozers and other heavy-tracked construction equipment generate

The GP EIR discussed impacts to population and housing on pages 4.14-1 through 4.14-10 and determined

Project-Specific Impacts
a) Induce substantial unplanned population growth in an area, either directly or indirectly?
No New Impact. This topic was evaluated in the GP EIR on pages 4.14-4 through 4.14-8 and was
determined to have a less than significant impact with the implementation of the goals and policies in the
GP. As discussed in the GP EIR, the reasonably foreseeable development in the City is projected to result in
approximately 22,000 new homes, 26,391 new jobs, and 75,765 new residents. Growth carried out under
the GP would increase the City’s total population by 45%, from 167,398 in 2022 to 243,154 in 2045,
which is above SCAG’s 2045 population forecast of 207,000 for 2045. Although substantial, the rate of
growth is expected to be planned and orderly, and to support existing and future employees, businesses,
and residents.
According to the SCAG forecasts for Commercial/Industrial Development and Job Growth, 2016-2045,
listed as Table 2-4 in the GP EIR, industrial projects in the City of Palmdale would generate one employee
per 850 square feet. As the proposed Project would build and operate 281,935 square feet of building
area, operation of the proposed Project would require approximately 331 employees. According to the GP
EIR, Palmdale has a current jobs-housing ratio of 0.8, which means that workers must travel to other
communities to find employment. Employees needed to operate the proposed Project are therefore
anticipated to come from within the Project region and a substantial in-migration of employees is not
anticipated to occur. Additionally, the City of Palmdale and Los Angeles County are both housing-dense

As discussed above, the LACWD 40 would supply water to the Project site. The LACWD 40 water supply is
composed of groundwater from District wells, non-potable recycled water, and water purchased from
Antelope Valley-East Kern Water Agency (AVEK). The Urban Water Management Plan (UWMP) for
LACOWD 40 details that, in 2020, water usage for the service area was 199 gallons per capita per day
(gpcd), which is below its 2020 target of 225 gpcd. LACOWD 40’s 2020 Urban Water Management Plan

The Palmdale Utilities Services Division (PUSD) manages the City’s wastewater discharge and sewage system.
Most of the collected wastewater, including the proposed Project, would flow to and be treated by the
Palmdale Water Treatment Plant (PWRP), which is managed in Los Angeles County Sanitation District #20.
The Palmdale Water Reclamation Plant provides primary, secondary, and tertiary treatment with a capacity
of 12 million gallons of wastewater per day and serves a population of approximately 150,000 people.
However, according to the PWRP Annual Monitoring Report 2020 and PWD UWMP, wastewater flows at
PWRP averaged 10.8 million gallons of wastewater per day. Therefore, PWRP has an excess treatment
capacity of approximately 1.2 million gallons per day.
Wastewater generation rates included in the GP EIR include generation factors developed by the City of
Los Angeles, and state that industrial development types generate approximately 80 gpd per 1,000 SF. As

accommodate the demand generated by the proposed Project based on the land use, size, and current

BACKGROUND

On January 13, 2006, the existing medical office complex was approved by a hearing
officer through Site Plan Review (SPR) 8-05-1. On July 11, 2013, CUP 13-009
(Resolution No. PC-2013-022) was approved by the Planning Commission to establish
an on-sale alcoholic beverage establishment with a Type 41 ABC license within an
approximately 1,610 square foot tenant space for use as a restaurant (Baracoa Cuban
Restaurant). Subsequently, the City Council approved Entertainment Permit No. 13-18
(Resolution No. CC 2014-002) on January 8, 2014, to allow for entertainment consisting
of a solo pianist, acoustical guitarist, small chamber ensemble, or a musician on an
occasional basis (no more than 12 days per month), which does not occupy more than

the Planning Commission approved CUP 15-010 (Resolution No. PC-2015-032), to
allow for a bar/nightclub with live entertainment and dancing within the existing bona

the restaurant and have requested the Planning Commission revoke the CUP.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The applicant is requesting approval of a Major Modification application to previously
approved CUP 13-009 to facilitate the construction of an 892-square-foot detached
covered patio to accommodate outdoor dining to an existing 1,610-square-foot bona
fide restaurant (Baracoa) located at 853 Auto Center Drive, Suite F. The Palmdale
Municipal Code (PMC) requires a Major Modification approval for the proposed project.

Baracoa currently has a Type 47 (Beer, Wine, and Distilled spirits) Department of
Alcoholic Beverage Control (ABC) license to sell beer, wine, and distilled spirits for on-
site sale and consumption of alcohol. The applicant has requested that the Planning
Commission consider the continued provision of live entertainment consisting of a solo
pianist, acoustical guitarist, small chamber ensemble, or a musician on an occasional
basis (no more than 12 days per month) within the existing building and the new
covered patio.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION

The applicant is requesting approval of CUP 23-005 and SPR 22-010 to facilitate the
construction of the proposed project.

The project approval consists of a request to develop two vacant parcels for the
construction of two commercial buildings totaling approximately 8,813 square feet
including convenience store and a fueling station with canopy, underground fuel tanks,
and a drive-through restaurant. In addition, the request to establish a Type 20 (Off-Sale
Beer and wine) Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control License. The project is located
at the southwest corner of Avenue O and 10th Street West (APNs: 3005-010-025 and -
026).

CUP 23-005 and SPR 22-010 includes the following:
   Constructing a 4,988 square-foot convenience store with alcohol sales;
   Constructing a 3,825 square-foot fueling station canopy with six fuel pumps; and,
   Constructing a 5,045 square-foot fast-food restaurant with a drive through.

The total building area for the proposed project is approximately 15,433 square feet
including both commercial buildings and fuel station canopy. The proposed project
includes improvements such as curb, gutter, sidewalks, parking, lighting improvements,
and landscaping needed to support the new development and including street
improvements across the project frontage along Avenue O and 10th Street West adjacent.
In addition, a new trash enclosure with cover is proposed for the proposed convenience
store and will not be visible from the street.

The proposed hours of operation are 24 hours seven days a week, however, the
convenience store hours of operation will be open to the public from 4:30 a.m. to 10:00
p.m. During the hours of 10:00 p.m. to 4:30 a.m. in-person transactions will be made
through a small transaction window.

In addition, the convenience store is proposing to sell tobacco products from behind the
counter in dedicated storage areas. Only the attendee will be able to access tobacco
products and comply with all State of California regulations for tobacco sales, as well as
the regulations of the Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC).

Access

Access will be provided from two driveways, one along the project frontage of Avenue O
and another along the project frontage of 10th Street West. Internal circulation will be
provided through a vehicular path around the fuel service canopy and a circular drive aisle
around the proposed drive through restaurant. The City Engineer and Los Angeles
County Fire Department have reviewed the project and determined that it is designed with
adequate access to accommodate safe vehicular flow. Furthermore, the City Engineer
has added Conditions of Approval to mitigate any potential impacts to access and on-site
circulation.

Architecture

The proposed materials and colors demonstrate earth tones. As depicted in Figure 3 the
architecture is mixture of different architectural elements that include various materials,
colors, and finishes that provide for variation and visual interest in the building elevations.
The building materials consist of aluminum cornice, stucco siding, manufactured stacked
stone, metal doors and frames, and aluminum canopies to accentuate secondary
entrances. Both commercial buildings incorporate three tower elements and modulation
of the facades to break large expansive planes. The colors and building massing have
been designed with careful consideration of the existing surrounding development and is
intended to be compatible and complementary. The trash enclosure exterior is of
decorative block, powder coated metal doors, and wood or formed steel painted to appear
as a wood trellis covering.

Conditional Use Permit - Convenience Store and Alcohol Sales, Off-Sale

CUP 23-005 is a request for approval of a convenience store with a Type 20 (Off-Sale
Beer and Wine), Department of Alcoholic Beverage Control License (ABC), which are
permitted uses with the approval of a CUP application within the Visitor Commercial (VC)
zone, as specified within PMC Chapter 17.48. As previously stated, the proposed hours
of operation are 24 hours seven days a week, however, the convenience store hours of
operation will be open to the public from 4:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. During the hours of 10:00
p.m. to 4:30 a.m. in-person transactions will be made through a small transaction window.
The convenience store must cease sale of alcoholic beverages between the hours of 2
a.m. and 6 a.m. daily. The approval of a Type 20 ABC license restricts the sale of alcohol
to Beer and Wine, the sale of distilled spirits is prohibited.

The sale, display, and storage of beer and wine will utilize less than ten percent of the
total floor area, (495 square feet) and is expected to constitute less than ten percent of
total sales volume for the convenience store. Within that total area, there are two beer
and wine displays within refrigerated coolers. There will be a walk-in cooler which will
have beer and wine for cold storage and there will also be an area of the storage room
dedicated to storage of beer and wine.

The use will also sell tobacco products behind the cash register and only accessible by
the convenience store employees. The employees and convenience store operators shall
comply with all State of California regulations and the PMC for the sale of tobacco
products. Furthermore, there have been conditions added to mitigate any potential
negative impacts to adjacent uses and neighborhood.

The applicant is proposing several security measures which include a 24-hour
surveillance system and 24-hour monitored alarm system. All points of entry will be
controlled with a key card and will be required to gain access to the building except

ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW

Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an Initial Study, to
determine whether the project would have a significant effect on the environment, has
been prepared. The Initial Study analyzed the potential for environmental impacts and all
topics were found to have either no impact, a less than significant impact, or a less than
significant impact with mitigation incorporated. Mitigation measures for biological
resources, cultural resources, geological resources, hydrology and water quality, and
tribal cultural resources were included to reduce impacts to a less than significant level.
In addition, the western Joshua tree has been designated a protected species under the
California Endangered Species Act. Therefore, any removal of western Joshua trees on

  SECTION 1. The Planning Commission hereby specifically finds that all the facts

  SECTION 2. The Planning Commission hereby finds as follows with respect to the
environmental document:

  A  Pursuant to the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA), an Initial
  Study, to determine whether the project would have a significant effect on
  the environment, has been prepared. The Initial Study analyzed the
  potential for environmental impacts and all topics were found to have either
  no impact, a less than significant impact, or a less than significant impact
  with mitigation incorporated. Mitigation measures for biological resources,
  cultural resources, geological resources, hydrology and water quality, and
  tribal cultural resources were included to reduce impacts to a less than
  significant level. In addition, the western Joshua tree has been designated
  a protected species under the California Endangered Species Act.
  Therefore, any removal of western Joshua trees on site must comply with
  all requirements from California Department of Fish and Wildlife (CDFW).
  The applicant must apply for an Incidental Take Permit in accordance with
  CDFW guidelines to address changes in State regulations relating to
  western Joshua trees. As such, an MND and MMRP was prepared and
  circulated in accordance with CEQA Guidelines.

  B  The custodian of records for the MND, and all other materials which
  constitute  the  record  of  proceedings  upon  which  the
  Planning Commission’s decision is based, is the Planning Manager of the
  City of Palmdale. These documents are available for public review in the
  Planning Division of the City of Palmdale located at 38250 Sierra Highway,
  Palmdale, California 93550, telephone (661) 267-5200.

  SECTION 3. Based upon substantial evidence presented to this Commission
during the above-referenced May 9, 2024, public hearing, including public testimony, and
written and oral staff report, this Commission specifically finds as follows:

  (a)  The design and layout of the proposed project or structures, in its final
  submitted form, or as conditioned, meets all of the following criteria, and the
  development is consistent with the City’s General Plan and any applicable
  specific plan; the development standards set forth in the Zoning Ordinance;
  and any applicable design guidelines. (SPR)

  The proposed project will provide access from two driveways, one along the
  project frontage of Avenue O and another along the project frontage of 10th
  Street West. Internal circulation will be provided through a vehicular path
  around the fuel service canopy and a circular drive aisle around the
  proposed drive through restaurant. The City Engineer and Los Angeles
  County Fire Department have reviewed the project and determined that it is
 Resolution No. PC-2024-008
Page 3

  designed with adequate access to accommodate safe vehicular flow.
  Furthermore, the City Engineer has added Conditions of Approval to
  mitigate any potential impacts to access and on-site circulation.

  The proposed materials and colors demonstrate earth tones. As depicted in
  Figure 3 the architecture is mixture of different architectural elements that
  include various materials, colors, and finishes that provide for variation and
  visual interest in the building elevations. The building materials consist of
  aluminum cornice, stucco siding, manufactured stacked stone, metal doors
  and frames, and aluminum canopies to accentuate secondary entrances.
  Both commercial buildings incorporate three tower elements and
  modulation of the facades to break large expansive planes. The colors and
  building massing have been designed with careful consideration of the
  existing surrounding development and is intended to be compatible and
  complementary. The trash enclosure exterior is of decorative block, powder
  coated metal doors, and wood or formed steel painted to appear as a wood
  trellis covering.

  Therefore, the development is consistent with the City’s General Plan and
  any applicable specific plan; the development standards set forth in the
  Zoning Ordinance; and any applicable design guidelines.

  (b)  The proposed use is consistent with the goals, policies, and objectives of
  the General Plan. (CUP)

  The General Plan Land Use designation of this site is Visitor Commercial
  (VC). The project is consistent with the intent of the VC General Plan land
  use designation and zone. The proposed use of a fuel station and drive-
  through restaurant are permitted uses within the VC zone. As such, no use
  permits are required for their respective operations. The convenience store
  and sale of alcohol are permitted with the approval of a CUP. The
  convenience store, fuel station, and drive-through uses will be required to
  comply with noise and illumination standards during all hours of operation
  as stated in the Conditions of Approval. As previously discussed above, the
  Type 20 (Off-Sale Beer and Wine) ABC license, is subject to the approval
  of a CUP application. If the CUP application were to be denied, the use of
  a fuel station and drive-through restaurant are permitted by right and would
  not be impacted.

  (c)  Typical operational characteristics include employees traveling to and from
  the site, customers purchasing fuel, snacks, and other items sold in the
  convenience store, drive-through and eat-in restaurant customers, and
  deliveries of merchandise and fuel. The operation of the convenience store
 Resolution No. PC-2024-008
Page 4

  and fuel station are both proposed to be 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
  Therefore, the uses are consistent with the goals, policies, and objectives
  of the General Plan.

  (d)  The site for the proposed use is adequate in size and shape to
  accommodate all development standards set forth in this Title. (SPR)

  The proposed commercial development is permitted within the VC zone and
  the site is physically suitable for the type of development proposed, which
  consists of a fuel service station, convenience store, and drive-through
  restaurant. The subject site is relatively flat and includes improvements for
  curb, gutter, and sidewalk improvements along the two street frontages,
  Avenue O and 10th Steet West. The proposed project meets the majority of
  relevant development standards. Those of which that do not comply are
  conditioned in the Conditions of Approval to comply during Building and
  Safety plan check. As such, the project site is capable of supporting the
  commercial development as described in Exhibits C and D and there are no
  known physical or environmental constraints.

  (e)  The proposed use and the on-going operation of the use will not have a
  substantial adverse effect on abutting vacant properties or the permitted
  use thereof, and will not generate excessive noise, vibration, traffic, or other
  disturbances, nuisances, or hazards. (CUP)

  The proposed convenience store hours of operation will be open to the
  public from 4:30 a.m. to 10:00 p.m. During the hours of 10:00 p.m. to 4:30
  a.m. in-person transactions will be made through a small transaction
  window. The convenience store must cease sale of alcoholic beverages
  between the hours of 2 a.m. and 6 a.m. daily. The approval of a Type 20
  ABC license restricts the sale of alcohol to Beer and Wine, the sale of
  distilled spirits is prohibited.

  The use will also sell tobacco products behind the cash register and only
  accessible by the convenience store employees. The employees and
  convenience store operators shall comply with all State of California
  regulations and the PMC for the sale of tobacco products. Furthermore,
  there have been conditions added to mitigate any potential negative impacts
  to adjacent uses and neighborhood.

  The applicant is proposing several security measures which include a 24-
  hour surveillance system and 24-hour monitored alarm system. All points of
  entry will be controlled with a key card and will be required to gain access
  to the building except through egress doors during open business hours.
 Resolution No. PC-2024-008
